name: Mud bath

card.summary: A soak in warm mineral mud at a spa or hot spring, used for relaxation and to leave skin feeling smoother and healthier.
card.aka: Mud therapy, fango, peloid bath, moor bath
card.note: Natural mud can carry microbes or radioactivity at some sites; trial research mostly concerns joint pain, not skin.

quick.overview:
A mud bath is a soak in warm, mineral-rich mud, typically a mix of natural clay and water, taken at hot springs, geothermal pools, lakes, seas or spas. A session lasts about 15 to 20 minutes. People take them for relaxation and for skin they describe as softer and healthier.

Spa tradition holds that heat boosts blood flow and that minerals benefit the skin. Published trials have mainly studied mud baths for osteoarthritis and fibromyalgia pain rather than for appearance.
quick.how: Visitors sit or lie in warm mud at a spa or natural site, then rinse. Courses of repeated sessions over days are common in European spa therapy.
quick.risks: Mud baths are generally low-risk, but at some sites mud can carry contaminants; for example, one Jamaican mud bath was linked to a rare amoebic infection, and radioactivity has been measured in some peat mud.

lead: A mud bath is a treatment in which a person soaks in warm mud, usually natural clay mixed with water, at hot springs, geothermal pools, inland seas or spas; sessions last roughly 15 to 20 minutes [1]. Claimed benefits include increased blood flow, easing muscle tension, relaxation and healthier-looking skin [1].
People use mud baths for skin and wellbeing. Research has largely concerned therapeutic mud, or peloid, baths for musculoskeletal disease, including systematic reviews on osteoarthritis [3][4].

chain: Heat and minerals applied to skin
angle.text: People use mud baths to leave skin feeling smooth and refreshed, and to relax. The skin benefits are traditional claims; studies focus on joint pain.

infobox: Dead Sea, Calistoga, Lake Techirghiol, mud volcanoes

paras: Mud for baths comes from lakes such as Techirghiol in Romania, seas such as the Dead Sea, hot springs such as Calistoga in California and mud volcanoes such as El Totumo in Colombia [1]. Wikipedia describes the claimed benefits as numerous, including heat increasing blood flow, minerals having healing properties, detoxification, relief of muscle pain and healthy skin [1].

A 2024 systematic review of 19 studies examined mud-pack and mud-bath therapy for osteoarthritis [3], and a 2021 meta-analysis assessed mud-bath therapy for knee osteoarthritis, linking effects to heat and the physicochemical properties of mud [4]. A 2021 systematic review summarized in Wikipedia concluded that mud baths cannot substitute for conventional therapy but may help as an add-on, relieving pain and stiffness [1]. A randomized single-blind trial with one-year follow-up compared mud-bath therapy with usual care in bilateral knee osteoarthritis [5]. Trials have also examined fibromyalgia, with one reporting effects on anti-aging markers [6]. Studies have measured hormonal responses in healthy subjects undergoing mud bath applications [7].
A report described Balamuthia mandrillaris infection linked to a therapeutic mud bath in Jamaica [8], and a study measured radioactivity of peat mud used in therapy [9].
